sentences.text: Lagenanectes richterae was an elasmosaurid plesiosaur, a marine reptile from the Lower Cretaceous of Lower Saxony, Germany, that reached an estimated length of about 8 meters (26 feet).

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was a fully grown individual showing ossification of cranial bones, vertebrae, and neural arches, and possessed a lower jaw with unique sidewards alveols and a platform with prominent dents on the underside.
The name Lagenanectes means "Leine swimmer," referring to the Leine river and the animal's swimming lifestyle.
Private collectors found the fossil in 1964 in a clay pit near Sarstedt.

Sven Sachs, Jahn J. Hornung, and Benjamin P. Kear erected the genus in 2017 after studying the fossil, and the specific name richterae honors Annette Richter for her contributions to paleontological exploration in Lower Saxony.
Grooves on the upper side of the skull may have accommodated electroreceptors used to locate prey.
Pathological alterations in the occiput and first neck vertebra may have been caused by an infection.
Research demonstrated that Lagenanectes richterae was an early member of the elasmosaurids.
Lagenanectes lived between 132.6 and 125.77 million years ago during the Hauterivian.
The age of the fossils is most probably the upper Hauterivian, though it might range from the lower Hauterivian to lower Barremian.
Cladistic analysis places Lagenanectes in a polytomy with an undescribed plesiosaur from the Speeton Clay and Callawayasaurus.
